title: Feature importance
story:
Once you have averaged five hundred trees, the model no longer contains a rule anyone can read, and the first question everybody asks is which inputs it is actually using. That question has no answer inside the model, so importance measures are attempts to recover it from outside.

The built-in answer for tree ensembles is to total up how much each feature reduced impurity across all the splits it appears in. It is free, since the quantities were computed during fitting, and it has two documented problems. It is strongly biased and favours high cardinality features, typically numerical features, over low cardinality features such as binary features or categorical variables with a small number of possible categories — a continuous column offers many candidate thresholds and so gets many chances to look useful. And it can give high importance to features that may not be predictive on unseen data when the model is overfitting, because it never leaves the fitted structure to check.

The intervention-based answer is better and is the one to reach for. Take the fitted model and a dataset, shuffle one column, score it again, and take the degradation as that column's contribution. Break the relationship between the feature and the target and see how much the model minded. It applies to any fitted estimator, it can be computed on held-out data, and it can use whatever metric you actually care about.

Two limitations matter more than they get credit for. Correlated inputs collapse the measure: when two features are correlated and one of them is permuted, the model still has access to the latter through its correlated feature, which results in a lower reported importance value for both features, though they might actually be important. Two columns carrying the same information can therefore both appear irrelevant, and a naive reading concludes that neither matters. The documented handling is to cluster features that are correlated and keep only one from each cluster.

And the deeper one, which the documentation states outright: this is not a property of the data. Features that are deemed of low importance for a bad model could be very important for a good model, and permutation importance does not reflect the intrinsic predictive value of a feature by itself but how important this feature is for a particular model. So an importance score is a fact about a fitted object. Read it as an answer to what is this model using, which it answers well, and not to what matters in this problem, which it does not answer at all.

problem.name: Model inspection
problem.shape: A fitted model is accurate and unreadable, and someone needs to know which inputs it depends on.
tell: the model is an ensemble and a stakeholder wants an explanation
features are being pruned by an importance ranking
two related columns both score near zero
the importance was read off the training fit
problem.move: Measure by intervention rather than inspection: shuffle a column on held-out data, rescore, and take the drop, using the metric the application cares about. Cluster correlated features and keep one per cluster before interpreting, and check the model is actually good before reading anything into what it relies on.
problem.invariant: An importance score describes how much a particular fitted model relies on a feature. It is a property of that model, not of the feature and not of the data.
problem.breaks: Correlation defeats the intervention. Shuffling one of two correlated columns leaves the model able to reach the same information through the other, so both report low importance while both may matter — the measure cannot distinguish a feature that is useless from one that is redundant.

cost.time: one rescoring pass per feature per repetition, which is far more expensive than the free impurity-based measure and is usually worth it
cost.beats: impurity-based importance, which is free and strongly biased toward high-cardinality features, and reading the model structure directly, which is not possible once it is an ensemble

worked.problem: What is a feature importance score a property of?
worked.reasoning:
A particular fitted model. Not the feature, not the dataset, and not the problem — and the documentation says so directly, because the mistake is common enough to warrant a warning.

The exact statement is that features deemed of low importance for a bad model could be very important for a good model, and that the measure does not reflect the intrinsic predictive value of a feature by itself but how important that feature is for a particular model. Two consequences follow immediately.

The first is that the model has to be good before its importances mean anything. If it has not learned the relationship, the inputs it happens to lean on tell you about its failure rather than about the data. So performance is established first, on held-out data, and only then is anything read into what the model relies on.

The second is that the ranking is not transferable. Fit a different model class and you can get a different ranking from the same data, and neither is wrong, because each describes its own object.

Then there are the two mechanical failures, which matter in practice.

Correlated features defeat the intervention. When two features are correlated and one is permuted, the model still reaches the same information through the other, so the reported importance is low for both — though they might actually be important. A naive reading concludes neither matters. The measure cannot separate useless from redundant, and the handling is to cluster correlated features and keep one per cluster before interpreting.

And the free impurity-based measure has a bias of its own: it is strongly biased and favours high cardinality features, typically numerical, over low cardinality ones such as binary features or categorical variables with few categories, because a continuous column offers many candidate thresholds and so many chances to appear useful. It can also give high importance to features that may not be predictive on unseen data when the model is overfitting, since it never leaves the fitted structure to check.

So the question it answers well is what is this model using, and I would use it for debugging — spotting a leaked column near the top, or a feature everyone expected to matter sitting at zero. The question it does not answer is what matters in this problem, and using a ranking to prune features treats it as though it did, which is also where the earlier point about entanglement bites: a feature's contribution depends on which others are present, so removing the lowest-ranked one is a hypothesis to test rather than a conclusion.

problem.practice: Compute both kinds of importance for the same fitted ensemble and compare the rankings, paying attention to where binary features sit in each. Then duplicate one informative column, refit, and watch both copies drop toward zero importance while the model's score does not change.

beats.broke: An ensemble of hundreds of trees makes decisions nobody can read, and the obvious question — which inputs is it actually using — has no answer inside the model.
beats.fix: Measure by intervention rather than inspection: shuffle one column, score the model again, and take the degradation as that column's contribution, which works for any fitted estimator and can be computed on held-out data.
beats.cost: The number describes a particular fitted model rather than the data, it collapses toward zero for correlated inputs because the model routes around a shuffled column, and the free impurity-based alternative is biased toward columns with many distinct values.

interview.q: What is a feature importance score a property of?
interview.trap: Treating it as a property of the data — a statement about which variables matter for the problem. It describes one fitted model, so a bad model's importances describe its failure, and two correlated columns can both read as irrelevant while both matter.
interview.answer:
A particular fitted model — not the feature, not the dataset, and not the problem. The documentation states this directly because the mistake is common: features deemed of low importance for a bad model could be very important for a good one, and the measure reflects not the intrinsic predictive value of a feature but how important it is for a particular model.

Two consequences follow. The model has to be good before its importances mean anything, because if it has not learned the relationship then whatever it leans on describes its failure rather than the data — so performance is established on held-out data first. And the ranking is not transferable: a different model class can give a different ranking from the same data, and neither is wrong, since each describes its own object.

Then two mechanical failures. Correlated features defeat the intervention: permuting one still leaves the model able to reach the information through the other, so both report low importance though both may matter, and the measure cannot separate useless from redundant. The documented handling is to cluster correlated features and keep one per cluster before interpreting. And the free impurity-based measure is strongly biased toward high-cardinality features — typically numerical ones over binary or small categorical ones — because a continuous column offers many candidate thresholds and so many chances to look useful, and it can also favour features that are not predictive on unseen data when the model is overfitting.

So the question it answers well is what this model is using, which makes it genuinely valuable for debugging — a leaked column near the top, or an expected feature sitting at zero. The question it does not answer is what matters in this problem, and pruning features by the ranking treats it as though it did — which also collides with entanglement, since a feature's contribution depends on which others are present.
